name: Mary Beth Norton
academic_discipline: History; American Colonial History; Women's History
primary_institution: Cornell University (Mary Donlon Alger Professor of American History)
specialization: Colonial New England; Salem witch crisis; gender and colonial society; frontier warfare and its social effects

major_works.title: In the Devil's Snare: The Salem Witchcraft Crisis of 1692
major_works.significance: Major recontextualization of Salem in terms of frontier war trauma, arguing that the Second Indian War's devastation of the Maine frontier was the primary generator of the specific crisis psychology of 1692

major_works.title: Liberty's Daughters: The Revolutionary Experience of American Women, 1750–1800
major_works.significance: Foundational study of American women's experience in the Revolutionary era; established Norton's approach to gender in colonial and early national history

core_argument: Norton's central contribution to witch-trial historiography is the frontier trauma thesis for Salem: the 1692 crisis was generated by the traumatic experience of King William's War (the Second Indian War, 1689-1697), which had devastated the Maine frontier and sent traumatized survivors and refugees into the Salem Village community. The afflicted girls and their families were disproportionately connected to the Maine frontier, and the prosecution's specific intensity and timing reflect wartime trauma psychology — the experience of invisible, lethal enemies who struck without warning — more than the community social tensions identified by Boyer and Nissenbaum or the property dynamics identified by Karlsen.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Salem examination records; Massachusetts Archives (frontier war records); Maine county records; Essex County court records
methodological_approach.analysis_target: The biographical and social connections between Salem accusers and the Maine frontier; the correlation between frontier experience and prosecution participation
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Biographical reconstruction; archival court records; Massachusetts colonial government records
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Social-historical contextualization: Norton situates the Salem crisis within the specific regional context of wartime colonial New England rather than treating it as a self-contained community event

key_contributions.claim: The 1692 crisis's specific intensity and timing reflected the traumatic experience of the Second Indian War: accusers disproportionately had Maine frontier connections, and the crisis psychology mirrored wartime anxiety about invisible enemies.
key_contributions.implication: Salem was not merely a community conflict or property dispute but a regional psychological crisis shaped by specific historical events that have been underweighted in previous scholarship.

key_contributions.claim: The Salem magistrates' willingness to accept spectral evidence and sustain prosecution reflected partly their guilt about their failure to protect the Maine frontier population — psychological stake that made skepticism about the prosecution politically and personally untenable.
key_contributions.implication: Elite participation in witch prosecution required not just ideological commitment but personal psychological investment.

engagement_with_primary_sources.trial_records: Norton's research added Maine frontier records to the Salem evidence base, providing biographical documentation of afflicted persons' frontier connections that previous Salem scholarship had not systematically explored.

alignment_with: Boyer and Nissenbaum (shared social-contextual approach; Norton supplements rather than replaces community-tension analysis)
Karlsen (Norton's work does not negate the property dimension but adds the frontier dimension)
creative_tension_with: Levack and European-focused scholarship (Norton's highly specific colonial context analysis does not translate to European comparative frameworks)

database_engagement.integration: Norton's analysis is referenced in the salem-1692-trials trial_event entry and provides additional context for the children-accused-of-witchcraft persecuted group entry.
database_engagement.analytical_weight: Norton provides the frontier-trauma contextual dimension that complements the community-tension (Boyer-Nissenbaum) and property-inheritance (Karlsen) analyses of Salem.

historiographical_significance: In the Devil's Snare reoriented Salem scholarship toward its regional context and the specific historical events that shaped its participants' psychology. The book is one of the most empirically grounded contributions to Salem historiography, adding substantive archival evidence (Maine frontier records) to the Salem debate rather than only reinterpreting existing evidence. Its frontier thesis has been broadly accepted as an important contextual factor while debate continues about its relative weight in explaining the crisis.
scholarly_disagreement: The strength of the causal connection between frontier trauma and Salem accusation is debated: the correlation Norton identifies is real but some historians question whether it rises to the level of causation. The mechanism by which frontier trauma translated into the specific form of witch accusation (rather than other crisis responses) is not fully explained.
source_method: Primary works: In the Devil's Snare (Knopf, 2002); Massachusetts Archives; Salem examination records; Maine county court records
